title: Ops ownership competitive briefing
content:
Purpose and audience:

This is a pragmatic briefing for field reps, SEs, and product marketers who need a tight, operations-focused narrative when selling Redwood against hyperscaler managed endpoints (e.g., SageMaker/Bedrock style, Vertex AI managed endpoints, Azure managed inference). Focus: the operational ownership story — not just feature parity — that matters to platform teams and engineering leaders trying to move LLMs into production.

TL;DR win themes (one-liners to memorize):
- We give customers the levers they actually need to control cost and latency in production — not opaque managed pricing and black-box scaling.
- We make graceful degradation a first-class behavior (fallback models, routing policies) so customer apps keep working during capacity spikes.
- We treat serving as software: predictable performance, token-level observability, and rollout primitives that fit engineering workflows.

Key customer pain signals to surface in discovery:
- "Our endpoint costs spike unpredictably when traffic increases or sequence lengths change."
- "We can’t debug why a request is slow — logs aren’t tied to tokens or requests."
- "Hyperscaler autoscaling isn’t tuned to LLM workloads; cold starts and queuing destroy p99 latency."
- "We can’t run our quantized or custom-compiled models in the managed offering."
- "Security/compliance teams want private deployments or strict VPC isolation, but sales says it’s expensive/slow to deploy."

Battlecard: quick comparisons (operational lens)
- Hyperscalers (AWS/GCP/Azure managed endpoints):
  - Strengths: broad cloud integrations (IAM, DBs, analytics), predictable enterprise procurement path, single-vendor cloud contracts.
  - Typical weakness for customers: opaque per-token/unit economics at scale, limited kernel/quantization control, autoscaling tuned for small stateless services (not continuous KV-cache/batched LLMs), limited per-token observability and rollout control.
- Redwood Inference:
  - Strengths: GPU-optimized runtime with production LLM batching and KV caching, per-token cost and latency telemetry, model variant routing and canary rollouts tied to evals, private/VPC and on-prem options for compliance, SLO-first autoscaling tuned for throughput vs latency tradeoffs.
  - Typical gap: hyperscalers win on 1-click integration with other cloud services and consolidated billing for customers already committed to a single cloud.

How to position (talk tracks by persona)
- Platform/Infra lead: "You need deterministic economics and control. With Redwood you can set batching and cache policies per-route, pin model variants, and see token-level cost. That makes forecasting and cost-allocation feasible — hyperscaler managed endpoints leave you guessing."
- ML engineer: "Deployments must support quantized kernels and library versions you rely on. Redwood provides model-variant management and kernel selection so your accuracy-cost tradeoffs are stable in prod."
- Product/PM: "When latency or availability matters for users, Redwood’s fallback routing and canary policies keep features live even when capacity is constrained."

Demo checklist (what to show in first 15 minutes)
- Live latency p99 dashboard filtering to a route + token-level cost breakdown for that route.
- A rollout: flip a canary to a quantized model variant and show traffic split, perf delta, and a regression alert firing on a prompt set.
- Routing policy: demonstrate automatic fallback from a high-cost variant to a lower-cost compatible variant during a simulated capacity event.
- Private deployment slide: short architecture diagram + typical timeline for VPC/on-prem install (emphasize security controls available).

Objection handling (short scripts)
- "We already have credits / volume discounts with our cloud provider": "Those discounts help early on, but they don’t solve variability in unit economics when usage grows or sequence-length distributions shift. We show customers exact per-route token economics so finance can allocate spend and engineers can tune batching."
- "Managed endpoints are simpler for us": "They are simpler for basic inference but LLM production is a different class of workload — the complexity shows up as unpredictable latency and cost as you scale. We remove that complexity by making the important knobs explicit and automatable."

Differentiators to quantify in conversations (metrics to gather before/at demo)
- Token-level cost delta vs hyperscaler baseline for representative workload (target to show: 30–60% lower unit cost after batching/caching/quantization recommendations).
- p99 latency improvement under load (target: 20–40% lower p99 for similar throughput due to KV caching and LLM-specific autoscaling).
- Reduction in outage windows due to graceful fallbacks (example: previously full outage for 1–2 hours vs Redwood’s 0–5 min degraded mode).

Suggested collateral to attach during follow-up
- Short 1-pager: "Ops ownership checklist" that maps Redwood controls to common cloud gaps (attach).
- Benchmark report for representative LLM (showing cost/latency at X qps and request length profile).
- Migration checklist + expected timeline and dependencies for Private deployment (security review, network, certs).

Tactical playbook for field reps (sequence)
1) Discovery call: capture sequence-length distribution, peak qps, existing SLA metrics, procurement constraints, and whether private deployment is required.
2) Benchmark ask: ask for a 1% traffic mirror or a small dataset of representative prompts — run a Redwood quick-bench to quantify cost/latency deltas.
3) Technical deep-dive: SE shows rollout, routing, and token telemetry; get security/compliance into a short call if private deployment needed.
4) Commercial: propose a hybrid path — start hosted with strict RBAC + routing, commit to reserved capacity pilot if unit economics look favorable, plan Private for full compliance.

Quick copy snippets (short outputs reps can paste into emails)
- "We give you the levers that matter for production-grade LLMs: deterministic unit economics, token-level visibility, and automated fallback policies so your features stay live during peak demand."
- "If you need VPC/on-prem control and kernel-level performance optimizations for quantized models, we can run a 2-week pilot and show exact cost/latency numbers for your workload."

Appendix: short checklist for qualifying a hyperscaler deal as vulnerable
- Customer cares about p99 latency under real-world sequences (not just average latency).
- Customer has multi-tenant teams who need cost allocation and per-route billing.
- Customer must meet compliance certifications or wants an air-gapped/on-prem option.
- Customer plans to use quantized/custom kernels or needs to tweak runtime parameters (batching, kv cache) for production.

End of doc — notes for next update: add a concise one-page handout that maps the hyperscaler ticket/incident lifecycle to Redwood’s incident playbook so SRE buyers can compare response expectations.
